# EDA using graphics {#sec-eda-ggplot}

```{r}
#| include: false

library(here)
library(ggplot2)

# The book's shared plot theme (this also loads the legend helpers)
Plot_theme <- source("functions/plot_theme.R")$value

# Read the cell data (one row per animal)
cell_data <- read.csv(here("project/AnalysisData/Cells_Gfap-Pdgfrb.csv"))

# Day as a category (one group per day, in time order) for the grouped plots
cell_data$DPI_f <- factor(cell_data$DPI, levels = c(0, 3, 7, 14, 30))

# Numbers quoted in the text, computed from the data so they cannot drift
n_obs <- nrow(cell_data)
n_vars <- ncol(cell_data)
n_day <- table(cell_data$DPI)
gfap_range <- range(cell_data$Gfap_IntDen)
pdgfrb_range <- range(cell_data$Pdgfrb_IntDen)
gfap_mean <- mean(cell_data$Gfap_IntDen)
gfap_sd <- sd(cell_data$Gfap_IntDen)
gfap_peak <- with(density(cell_data$Gfap_IntDen), x[which.max(y)])
pdgfrb_peak <- with(density(cell_data$Pdgfrb_IntDen), x[which.max(y)])
gfap_mean_day <- tapply(cell_data$Gfap_IntDen, cell_data$DPI, mean)
gfap_med_day <- tapply(cell_data$Gfap_IntDen, cell_data$DPI, median)
gfap_sd_day <- tapply(cell_data$Gfap_IntDen, cell_data$DPI, sd)
pdgfrb_mean_day <- tapply(cell_data$Pdgfrb_IntDen, cell_data$DPI, mean)
pdgfrb_med_day <- tapply(cell_data$Pdgfrb_IntDen, cell_data$DPI, median)
pdgfrb_sd_day <- tapply(cell_data$Pdgfrb_IntDen, cell_data$DPI, sd)

# Day 30 GFAP: the widest gap between neighbouring animals (a low group and a high group)
gfap_d30 <- sort(cell_data$Gfap_IntDen[cell_data$DPI == 30])
gap_at <- which.max(diff(gfap_d30))
d30_low_max <- gfap_d30[gap_at]
d30_high_min <- gfap_d30[gap_at + 1]
d30_n_low <- gap_at
d30_n_high <- length(gfap_d30) - gap_at

# Straight-line fit of GFAP on day, only to see where the line sits at day 0
gfap_line_d0 <- unname(coef(lm(Gfap_IntDen ~ DPI, data = cell_data))[1])

# Correlation between the two markers, pooled and within each day
r_pooled <- cor(cell_data$Gfap_IntDen, cell_data$Pdgfrb_IntDen)
r_day <- sapply(split(cell_data, cell_data$DPI),
                function(s) cor(s$Gfap_IntDen, s$Pdgfrb_IntDen))
```

Back in @sec-eda-first-look we read the table, and in @sec-eda-data-quality and @sec-eda-missing-data we made sure we could trust it. The table told us what is in `cell_data`. It could not tell us what the data *look like*, and that is the question I was itching to ask the whole time. You have probably been here before: a spreadsheet of fluorescence quantifications, a mean and a standard deviation per group already sitting in a slide, and a nagging feeling that the numbers are hiding something. This chapter is where we stop reading and start drawing.

::: {style="text-align: center"}
***What does the pile of measurements actually look like?***
:::

The data come from my own work on glial scarring after experimental cerebral ischemia, a model I used for almost a decade. We met the study in @sec-intro-applied-modeling; here we open the whole dataset and look at two markers, `Gfap_IntDen` (GFAP integrated density, an astroglial marker) and `Pdgfrb_IntDen` (PDGFR-β integrated density, a pericyte marker), quantified in FIJI [@schindelin2012] across five days post-ischemia (DPI). Everything is drawn with `ggplot2` [@wickham2016], which builds a figure by stacking layers, one per question you want to put to the data. The map for this part is in the introduction to exploratory data analysis, and @sec-eda-summary will collect what we learn here into one running list; for now we ask three questions in order, each answered by a different kind of figure: how are the values distributed, how do they change with time, and do the two markers move together?

## The data

Here are the first rows of `cell_data`, printed with `gt` [@gt] so they look the same in the web and the PDF editions (@tbl-cell_data_tbl). The file is read with `here` [@here], which finds it from the project root, so the code runs on any machine without editing paths.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cell_data_tbl
#| tbl-cap: First rows of `cell_data`, the table used for the graphical exploration

library(gt)

# The first six rows, as a table
gt(head(cell_data))
```

The table has `r n_vars` columns and `r n_obs` rows, one per animal, with `r paste(n_day, collapse = ", ")` animals at days `r paste(names(n_day), collapse = ", ")`. We will keep the focus on the two integrated-density columns and on `DPI`. With about ten animals per day, you will see that every figure below shows the individual animals. That is not a stylistic whim; it is the point of the chapter.

## Looking at the distribution: density plots

If the word *distribution* feels abstract, picture the measurements of all the animals dropped onto a number line like grains of sand. Where the pile is tall, many animals share that value; where it thins out, few do. A [density plot]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} is the outline of that pile. The outline tells you what a mean and a standard deviation cannot: whether you have one hill, two, or a hill with a long tail (@fig-eda-ggplot-bell-jar shows why that matters).

Before the first plot, one piece of housekeeping. Every figure in this book uses the same theme, `Plot_theme`, built once with ggplot2's `theme()` function and stored in `functions/plot_theme.R`. We load it at the top of each chapter so the typography and axes look the same everywhere instead of coming from a different author each time. It sits in the hidden setup chunk of this chapter, together with the legend helpers explained in @sec-appendix-figures.

::: {.callout-note title="Where the look of these figures comes from"}
A great deal of how I think about showing data comes from Yan Holtz, through his work on [GitHub](https://github.com/holtzy) and his data visualization project, [Dataviz Inspiration](https://www.dataviz-inspiration.com/). AI assistants then helped me improve the graphics and discover new tools to build them, in an ecosystem that changes quickly.
:::

For a first look I choose a density over a histogram because its outline does not depend on where the bars happen to start (it does have a smoothing setting of its own, the bandwidth, which we turn on purpose near the end of this chapter), and I choose either over a bar with an error whisker because a whisker cannot show that a distribution has two humps. We use `ggplot2::geom_density()` and place the two markers side by side with `patchwork` [@patchwork], whose `+` operator joins plots and whose `plot_annotation()` adds the A and B tags you see in papers. Each plot is a short recipe: `data` names the table, `aes()` says which column goes on the x axis (density supplies the y axis itself), `geom_density()` draws the outline, `labs()` writes the labels and `Plot_theme` dresses it.

One decision about color deserves a sentence, because it will repeat all chapter. PDGFR-β is always vermillion and GFAP always blue (Okabe-Ito colors, as in @wilke2019). The same marker keeps the same color in every figure, so you never need a legend to remember who is who, and the pair stays distinguishable for readers with the most common forms of color blindness and in a grayscale print of the PDF, which a red-green pair does not.

```{r}
#| label: fig-cell_data_dens_EDA
#| fig-cap: Distribution of PDGFR-β and GFAP integrated density across all animals (density plots)
#| fig-alt: Two density plots side by side. Both are right-skewed, with a main peak at low to middle values and a long tail toward high values.
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(patchwork)

# One color per marker, reused in every figure of this chapter
Pdgfrb_color <- "#D55E00"
Gfap_color <- "#0072B2"

# Density of PDGFR-β integrated density
Pdgfrb_dens <- ggplot(data = cell_data, aes(x = Pdgfrb_IntDen)) +
  geom_density(fill = Pdgfrb_color, alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "PDGFR-β", x = "PDGFR-β integrated density", y = "Density") +
  Plot_theme

# Density of GFAP integrated density
Gfap_dens <- ggplot(data = cell_data, aes(x = Gfap_IntDen)) +
  geom_density(fill = Gfap_color, alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "GFAP", x = "GFAP integrated density", y = "Density") +
  Plot_theme

# Join the two plots side by side and tag them A and B
Pdgfrb_dens + Gfap_dens + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")
```

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read this figure"}
Look at the height first: the tallest part of the outline is where most animals sit. Then look at the sides. A symmetric hill has two similar tails; a long tail on one side means a few animals sit far from the rest. Finally, count the humps. One hump says "one population"; two say "look for a reason" (two cell types, two days, two batches). Nothing here asks whether a curve is "significant"; you are reading a shape.
:::

@fig-cell_data_dens_EDA gives a first answer. Both markers have their main peak at low to middle values (around `r round(pdgfrb_peak)` for PDGFR-β and `r round(gfap_peak)` for GFAP) and a long right-hand tail: PDGFR-β runs from `r round(pdgfrb_range[1])` to `r round(pdgfrb_range[2])` and GFAP from `r round(gfap_range[1])` to `r round(gfap_range[2])`. Neither looks like a bell.

### Is the data normally distributed?

The question every reviewer eventually asks. It is worth answering with a picture, not a test. To see how far a bell curve is from our data, let us draw the normal curve with the *same mean and standard deviation* as GFAP (mean `r round(gfap_mean)`, standard deviation `r round(gfap_sd)`) over the observed density, so the comparison is the fairest one the normal curve can get (@fig-cell_data_normal_EDA). We draw it with `stat_function()`, which lays any mathematical curve over a plot.

```{r}
#| label: fig-cell_data_normal_EDA
#| fig-cap: Observed GFAP density (blue) against the normal curve with the same mean and standard deviation (vermillion line)
#| fig-alt: A blue density of GFAP integrated density with a long right tail, and a symmetric vermillion bell curve drawn over it. The bell curve extends below zero, where there are no observations, and misses the peak of the data.
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# Observed GFAP density (filled) with the normal curve of equal mean and spread on top
Gfap_dens_normal <- ggplot(data = cell_data, aes(x = Gfap_IntDen)) +
  geom_density(fill = Gfap_color, alpha = 0.5) +
  stat_function(
    fun = dnorm,
    args = list(mean = gfap_mean, sd = gfap_sd),
    color = Pdgfrb_color,
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  labs(x = "GFAP integrated density", y = "Density") +
  Plot_theme

Gfap_dens_normal
```

The vermillion line in @fig-cell_data_normal_EDA is the best bell the mean and standard deviation can build, and it still fits badly. It spills below zero, where an integrated density cannot go, and its peak sits to the side of where the animals actually pile up (@fig-eda-ggplot-bell-jar).

![A normal curve is a neat bell jar for your data, until the data have a long tail. Forced over skewed measurements, part of them sticks out.](images/eda-ggplot_bell-jar-over-skewed-clay.png){#fig-eda-ggplot-bell-jar fig-align="center" width="90%" fig-alt="Watercolor sketch of a symmetric glass bell jar on a wooden bench covering a lumpy mound of ochre clay that is steep on the left, with a long thin tail of clay sticking out from under the right edge of the jar and trailing along the bench."}

Now the fair-minded caveat, which I wish someone had told me earlier. This picture pools animals from five different days, and we are going to see in a moment that the days sit at very different levels. A pile made of five shifted piles will look lopsided even if each day on its own were perfectly bell-shaped. What a linear model assumes is also subtler than "the column is normal": it concerns the *residuals*, the variation left over once the predictors are accounted for, and we check that explicitly in @sec-linear-regression-assumptions. So the honest reading of @fig-cell_data_normal_EDA is not "the data fail a normality test". It is "a mean and a standard deviation of the pooled column are a poor description of it, so summarize by group and look at the shape". (If you are wondering why I do not run a Shapiro-Wilk test here, @sec-appendix-assumption-tests shows with simulated data what such tests can and cannot do.) The same argument answers the reader who says that with more animals the shape would become normal: more animals would sharpen the outline of the pile, not remove the structure that makes it lopsided.

## Conditioning on time: scatter plots

Which brings us to the structure. The pooled picture ignores the one variable that organizes this experiment. `DPI` records the day after ischemia on which each animal was perfused, stained and imaged, so it takes five values: 0, 3, 7, 14 and 30, five snapshots of the unfolding of the glial scar. Ignoring it would be like averaging a time-lapse video into one blurry frame. The next question is then:

::: {style="text-align: center"}
***How does my data change with time after ischemia?***
:::

There are two honest ways to treat `DPI`, and they answer different questions. As a *number*, it asks about trends: does the marker go up as days pass? As a *category* (five groups), it asks about distributions: what does the pile look like on each day? We take the numeric view in this section, with [scatter plots]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}, and the categorical one in the next.

A scatter plot is the right figure for "does y change with x", because position on both axes carries the information and every animal is one dot. We add two things to the dots. `geom_smooth(method = lm)` draws the best-fit straight line, the one that stays as close as possible to the points (we make "as close as possible" precise in @sec-linear-regression-what), with a band for its uncertainty. And `ggExtra::ggMarginal()` [@ggextra] draws small histograms and densities on the borders, so we see the two distributions of @fig-cell_data_dens_EDA again, now in the margins of the plot. `cowplot` [@cowplot] arranges the two marked-up panels in a row.

```{r}
#| label: fig-cell_data_scatter_EDA
#| fig-cap: PDGFR-β and GFAP integrated density against days post-ischemia (scatter plots with a straight-line fit and marginal distributions)
#| fig-alt: Two scatter plots of integrated density against days post-ischemia (0, 3, 7, 14 and 30), one for PDGFR-β in vermillion and one for GFAP in blue. Each has a black straight line with a shaded band, and marginal histograms on the top and right. Points at 0 and 3 days lie low and close together; later days are higher and more spread out.
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| results: false

library(cowplot)
library(ggExtra)

# PDGFR-β against day, with a straight-line fit
Pdgfrb_scatter <- ggplot(data = cell_data, aes(x = DPI, y = Pdgfrb_IntDen)) +
  geom_smooth(method = lm, color = "black", fill = Pdgfrb_color, se = TRUE) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 3, 7, 14, 30)) +
  labs(x = "Days post-ischemia (DPI)", y = "PDGFR-β integrated density") +
  Plot_theme

# Marginal distributions on the borders
Pdgfrb_scatter_Marginal <- ggMarginal(
  Pdgfrb_scatter, type = "densigram",
  colour = "black", fill = Pdgfrb_color, alpha = 0.9
)

# Same figure for GFAP
Gfap_scatter <- ggplot(data = cell_data, aes(x = DPI, y = Gfap_IntDen)) +
  geom_smooth(method = lm, color = "black", fill = Gfap_color, se = TRUE) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 3, 7, 14, 30)) +
  labs(x = "Days post-ischemia (DPI)", y = "GFAP integrated density") +
  Plot_theme

Gfap_scatter_Marginal <- ggMarginal(
  Gfap_scatter, type = "densigram",
  colour = "black", fill = Gfap_color, alpha = 0.9
)

# Place both panels in one row
cowplot::plot_grid(Pdgfrb_scatter_Marginal, Gfap_scatter_Marginal, nrow = 1, ncol = 2)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read this figure"}
First, the direction of the cloud: does it climb, fall or stay flat? Second, the line: is it a fair summary of where the dots are *at every day*, or does it pass above or below whole groups of them? Third, the width of the cloud at each day: a cloud that is narrow at one end and wide at the other is a different problem from a cloud that is simply shifted. The margins tell you the same story collapsed onto one axis. The line is a drawing aid, not a fitted model yet; we fit models in @sec-linear-regression-single-continuous.
:::

Both markers climb with time (@fig-cell_data_scatter_EDA), which is what I expect as someone who has looked at a lot of ischemic tissue: GFAP and PDGFR-β go up as the glial and neurovascular response builds. But the straight line is not telling the whole story, and three details say so.

**The line does not follow the animals.** For PDGFR-β, the animals at 0 and 3 DPI sit well below the line (median `r round(pdgfrb_med_day["0"])` and `r round(pdgfrb_med_day["3"])`, against `r round(pdgfrb_med_day["14"])` at 14 DPI), so the early days are overestimated and the middle is underestimated. For GFAP the line crosses day 0 at about `r round(gfap_line_d0)` while the day-0 animals sit near `r round(gfap_mean_day["0"])`, so it misses all of them. GFAP also stops climbing: its mean is `r round(gfap_mean_day["14"])` at 14 DPI and `r round(gfap_mean_day["30"])` at 30 DPI, a plateau and a dip that no straight line can follow. Nothing is wrong with the line as arithmetic; it is the wrong *shape* for these data, and that is what we explore next in @sec-linear-regression-assumptions.

**The spread is not constant.** At 0 and 3 DPI the animals are tightly packed (the standard deviation of GFAP is `r round(gfap_sd_day["0"])` and `r round(gfap_sd_day["3"])`), and from day 7 on they scatter widely (`r round(gfap_sd_day["7"])` at 7 DPI). PDGFR-β shows the same widening, from `r round(pdgfrb_sd_day["0"])` at day 0 to `r round(pdgfrb_sd_day["30"])` at day 30. Is that biologically sensible? Entirely. At baseline the tissue is stable and what varies is staining, imaging and natural differences between animals. After the injury, lesion size, feeding, recovery and the animal's own response add their own variability, so identical surgeries produce quite different scars. Statisticians call this unequal spread [heteroskedasticity]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} (its opposite, a constant spread, is *homoskedasticity*), and think of the bell of a trumpet: narrow at the mouthpiece, wide at the other end (@fig-eda-ggplot-trumpet). One straight line and one variance cannot describe both ends. Knowing the biology lets us *predict* this pattern before we see it, which is the best use of expertise in EDA; @sec-linear-regression-assumptions turns it into a checkable assumption, and @sec-multivariate-distributional-regression shows how to model the spread itself instead of ignoring it.

![A trumpet starts narrow and ends wide, like the spread of our data over time: tight at the start, scattered later. One straight line, and one variance, can't describe both ends.](images/eda-ggplot_trumpet-widening-spread.png){#fig-eda-ggplot-trumpet fig-align="center" width="90%" fig-alt="Watercolor sketch of a brass trumpet lying on a wooden bench. Small teal and ochre dots come out along it, forming a tight narrow line near the mouthpiece and spreading into a wide scattered fan beyond the bell, with a thin straight arrow along the trumpet's axis."}

**The margins show the skew.** The marginal densities on the right of each panel repeat what @fig-cell_data_dens_EDA showed: more animals at lower intensities and a long reach toward high ones. Note that this is the pooled pile again, so it mixes days.

With only the scatter plots we can say three things: a straight line is a poor description of the trend, the spread grows with time, and the pooled values are right-skewed. They are leads, not conclusions. We have not fitted a model, and, as we will see in @sec-eda-summary, what a plot proposes a model must still decide.

## Conditioning on time as a category: raincloud plots

Now treat `DPI` as five groups, which is already done in the hidden setup chunk (`DPI_f`, a factor in time order). The question becomes about shapes, group by group:

::: {style="text-align: center"}
***What does the distribution look like on each day?***
:::

The figure I reach for here is the [raincloud plot]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}. The name comes from its anatomy: a half-density on one side is the *cloud*, and the individual animals scattered beneath it are the *rain*, with a boxplot between them to give the median and the middle half. Three packages build it: `ggdist::stat_halfeye()` [@ggdist; @kay2024] draws the cloud, `ggplot2::geom_boxplot()` the box, and `gghalves::geom_half_point()` [@gghalves] the rain. A diamond, drawn with `stat_summary()`, marks the mean.

Why this form and not the bar with asterisks that fills most papers? A bar keeps one number per group and throws everything else away: the spread, the shape, and the fact that there are only `r min(n_day)` to `r max(n_day)` animals behind each group. A boxplot keeps five numbers and still cannot show two humps. The raincloud shows all of it at once. A design tip you can reuse: whenever a group has fewer than about thirty observations, show every one of them. (More on these choices, and on what the usual alternatives hide, in @sec-appendix-figures.)

```{r}
#| label: fig-cell_data_rain_EDA
#| fig-cap: PDGFR-β and GFAP integrated density by day post-ischemia (raincloud plots; the diamond is the group mean)
#| fig-alt: Two raincloud plots with days 0, 3, 7, 14 and 30 on the x axis. For each day there is a half-density cloud, a boxplot and the individual animals as points to the left, with a colored diamond for the mean. PDGFR-β rises steadily and spreads out with time. GFAP rises to day 7 or 14 and drops slightly at day 30, where it has two groups of animals.
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(ggdist)
library(gghalves)

# PDGFR-β by day: cloud, box, rain and mean
Pdgfrb_raincloud <- ggplot(data = cell_data, aes(x = DPI_f, y = Pdgfrb_IntDen)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5, width = 0.6, .width = 0,
               justification = -0.3, point_colour = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.2, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_half_point(side = "l", range_scale = 0.4, alpha = 0.5) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 18, size = 4,
               color = Pdgfrb_color) +
  labs(x = "Days post-ischemia (DPI)", y = "PDGFR-β integrated density") +
  Plot_theme

# GFAP by day, same layers
Gfap_raincloud <- ggplot(data = cell_data, aes(x = DPI_f, y = Gfap_IntDen)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5, width = 0.6, .width = 0,
               justification = -0.3, point_colour = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.2, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_half_point(side = "l", range_scale = 0.4, alpha = 0.5) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 18, size = 4,
               color = Gfap_color) +
  labs(x = "Days post-ischemia (DPI)", y = "GFAP integrated density") +
  Plot_theme

# Side by side, tagged
Pdgfrb_raincloud + Gfap_raincloud + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")
```

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read this figure"}
Read each day as a small landscape. The points on the left are the animals themselves; count them to remember how few there are. The cloud above is the outline of that pile (the same idea as a density plot, now one per day), so a cloud with two humps is a group that behaves like two groups. The box gives the median (black line) and the middle half of the animals. The diamond is the mean: when it sits on the median and in the middle of the cloud, a mean describes the group; when it floats away from both, it does not.
:::

@fig-cell_data_rain_EDA answers what the scatter plots could not. Both markers are tight at 0 and 3 DPI and spread out afterwards, as before, but now we see how: at 30 DPI PDGFR-β ranges from about `r round(min(cell_data$Pdgfrb_IntDen[cell_data$DPI == 30]))` to `r round(max(cell_data$Pdgfrb_IntDen[cell_data$DPI == 30]))`, a long reach with no gap. GFAP at 30 DPI looks different. Its `r d30_n_low` lowest animals sit at `r round(d30_low_max)` or below, then there is an empty stretch up to `r round(d30_high_min)`, and the other `r d30_n_high` animals lie above it. With eleven animals I would not swear to two populations, but it is an honest hint of two kinds of response (a more and a less reactive scar), and it is a hint a bar plot would never have shown. The mean, `r round(gfap_mean_day["30"])`, sits inside that gap, where there is hardly an animal; the median, `r round(gfap_med_day["30"])`, lands in the upper group. Neither describes a typical animal, and the mean is the worse of the two (@fig-eda-ggplot-raincloud). The same drift shows for PDGFR-β at 14 DPI, where the mean (`r round(pdgfrb_mean_day["14"])`) and the median (`r round(pdgfrb_med_day["14"])`) have separated, while at 0 and 3 DPI they nearly coincide.

![A raincloud with two humps. The mean, the little diamond, floats in the gap between them, exactly where there is no cloud, no rain, and no data.](images/eda-ggplot_two-hump-raincloud.png){#fig-eda-ggplot-raincloud fig-align="center" width="90%" fig-alt="Watercolor sketch of two pale teal clouds side by side with a gap between them, each raining teal and ochre drops onto a strip of grass below. An ochre diamond-shaped kite floats alone in the gap, where there is neither cloud nor rain."}

### Revisiting the question: is the data normally distributed?

We can now answer the question we left open, and answer it better. Within each day the shapes are mostly not bell-like either, and the clearest sign is the GFAP distribution at 30 DPI. But I want to keep the reason for asking straight. We do not ask about shape to satisfy a rule written by statisticians whose names we cannot recall, or a reviewer's checklist. We ask because the shape decides how we should *summarize* the group and compare groups: a mean and a standard deviation are a fair summary of a hill and a poor one of two hills or a long tail. If the data do not behave, the remedy is a different model (one with a family and a spread that suit them), not a different test run on the same assumptions. The book returns to this question as we choose likelihoods for counts, proportions and skewed positive values, starting in @sec-count-regression and @sec-beta-robust-regression, and it checks the modeling assumptions properly, on the residuals, in @sec-mcmc-model-checking and @sec-linear-regression-assumptions.

No statistical model is perfect, and none describes a tissue with infinite precision. Some are more useful than others for the data in front of you, and exploring with your eyes first is how you pick.

## Do the two markers move together? An interactive scatter plot

The last question connects the two markers we have been drawing side by side.

::: {style="text-align: center"}
***What is the association between PDGFR-β and GFAP?***
:::

Both rise with time, so I expect them to correlate. But the correlation across the whole dataset is a blend of two things: the markers moving together *within* a day, and both moving with the day. Let us plot one marker against the other and color the animals by `DPI`, so the blend comes apart. (If you want to compare *every* pair of variables rather than this one, @sec-eda-ggpairs does that with a single call.)

A static scatter plot would already show the trend, but it hides something we care about: *which* dot is which animal and day, and where a suspicious one came from, the anomaly-hunting that is one of the core jobs of EDA. Instead of cluttering the plot with fifty labels, we let the reader hover. That is the only reason to reach for interactivity here, and the tool is `ggiraph` [@ggiraph], which turns ggplot layers into hoverable ones. The ingredients are `tooltip` (the text shown on hover, here GFAP, PDGFR-β and DPI), `data_id` (a unique tag for each point), and the `_interactive` versions of `geom_point()` and `geom_smooth()`. For color we use a viridis scale [@viridis], which is perceptually uniform, readable for colorblind viewers, and a natural fit for an ordered quantity such as the day.

This is also the first figure in the book where the web and PDF editions truly differ. A page cannot hover, so the PDF gets the same plot without tooltips, in a twin chunk, instead of a broken widget or a blank gap.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

```{r}
#| label: fig-cell_data_scatter_covariance_EDA
#| fig-cap: GFAP against PDGFR-β integrated density, colored by day post-ischemia (interactive; hover over a point to see its values)
#| fig-alt: Scatter plot of PDGFR-β against GFAP integrated density with points colored from dark purple (day 0) to yellow (day 30) and one black straight line. Day 0 and day 3 points are near the origin and tightly packed; later days spread widely and mostly lie above the line at the upper end.
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5.5
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(ggiraph)
library(viridis)

# Interactive scatter: each point carries a tooltip and an id
Pdgfrb_Gfap_scatter <- ggplot(
  data = cell_data,
  aes(
    x = Gfap_IntDen,
    y = Pdgfrb_IntDen,
    color = DPI_f,
    tooltip = paste("GFAP:", round(Gfap_IntDen), "<br>PDGFR-β:", round(Pdgfrb_IntDen),
                    "<br>DPI:", DPI),
    data_id = rownames(cell_data)
  )
) +
  geom_point_interactive(size = 3) +
  scale_color_viridis(discrete = TRUE, option = "viridis", name = "DPI") +
  geom_smooth_interactive(
    tooltip = "Linear relation",
    data_id = "Linear relation",
    method = "lm", color = "black", se = FALSE
  ) +
  labs(x = "GFAP integrated density", y = "PDGFR-β integrated density") +
  Plot_theme +
  # Legend above the plot, in one row
  legend_top()

# Turn the ggplot into a hoverable widget (girafe_book keeps the book's figure size rule)
girafe_book(Pdgfrb_Gfap_scatter, width_svg = 6, height_svg = 5.5)
```

Hover over any point in @fig-cell_data_scatter_covariance_EDA to read its exact values and day.

:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

```{r}
#| label: fig-cell_data_scatter_covariance_EDA-pdf
#| fig-cap: GFAP against PDGFR-β integrated density, colored by day post-ischemia (static edition; the web edition lets you hover over each point)
#| fig-alt: Scatter plot of PDGFR-β against GFAP integrated density with points colored from dark purple (day 0) to yellow (day 30) and one black straight line. Day 0 and day 3 points are near the origin and tightly packed; later days spread widely.
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5.5
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(viridis)

# Same plot as the interactive one, without tooltips, for the PDF edition
Pdgfrb_Gfap_scatter_static <- ggplot(
  data = cell_data,
  aes(x = Gfap_IntDen, y = Pdgfrb_IntDen, color = DPI_f)
) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "black", se = FALSE) +
  scale_color_viridis(discrete = TRUE, option = "viridis", name = "DPI") +
  labs(x = "GFAP integrated density", y = "PDGFR-β integrated density") +
  Plot_theme +
  legend_top()

Pdgfrb_Gfap_scatter_static
```

@fig-cell_data_scatter_covariance_EDA-pdf is the static twin of the interactive figure in the web edition, where you can hover over each point.

:::

Pooled over all animals the two markers correlate moderately (r = `r sprintf("%.2f", r_pooled)`), but look at the colors. The day-0 animals (dark purple) are packed near the origin and the day-3 animals just beyond them; the later days (green to yellow) spread across the plot. Within a single day the relationship is far from uniform: the correlation is `r sprintf("%.2f", r_day["0"])` at day 0, `r sprintf("%.2f", r_day["3"])` at day 3, `r sprintf("%.2f", r_day["7"])` at day 7, `r sprintf("%.2f", r_day["14"])` at day 14 and `r sprintf("%.2f", r_day["30"])` at day 30. With ten animals per day these within-day correlations are rough, and I would not read much into a single one. But the pattern they make is the point: the straight line summarizes a relationship that is mostly *time moving both markers*, and it does not describe any one day well. Letting the line differ by day is what we call an interaction, and @sec-linear-regression-multiple fits the one the design allows.

## Two more shapes, borrowed: when the smoothing and the pooling matter

`cell_data` has taught us a lot, but two lessons are easier to see in other people's data, and a package I used in @sec-eda-missing-data, `NeuroDataSets` [@neurodatasets], has two small real datasets that make them vivid. I use them only in this section. The first is about how much a histogram or a density can *invent* or *hide*. The second is about what happens when a figure pools regions that behave differently, a cousin of pooling days.

```{r}
#| include: false

library(NeuroDataSets)

# Two real datasets shipped with the NeuroDataSets package
data("guineapig_neuro_df", package = "NeuroDataSets")
data("aba_phenotype_data_df", package = "NeuroDataSets")
gp <- guineapig_neuro_df
aba <- aba_phenotype_data_df

# Order the regions by their median GFAP so the figures read from low to high
aba$region <- reorder(aba$structure_acronym.x, aba$ihc_gfap_ffpe,
                      FUN = median, na.rm = TRUE)

# Numbers quoted in the text, computed from the data so they cannot drift
dens_peaks <- function(x, ...) {
  d <- density(x, ...)
  d$x[which(diff(sign(diff(d$y))) == -2) + 1]
}
gp_n <- nrow(gp)
gp_mean <- mean(gp$y)
gp_sd <- sd(gp$y)
gp_median <- median(gp$y)
gp_peaks <- dens_peaks(gp$y)
gp_peaks_narrow <- dens_peaks(gp$y, adjust = 0.4)
gp_n_top <- sum(gp$y > 26)
gp_max <- max(gp$y)
aba_n <- nrow(aba)
aba_n_region <- table(aba$region)
aba_gfap_med <- tapply(aba$ihc_gfap_ffpe, aba$region, median, na.rm = TRUE)
aba_iba1_med <- tapply(aba$ihc_iba1_ffpe, aba$region, median, na.rm = TRUE)
aba_na_gfap <- sum(is.na(aba$ihc_gfap_ffpe))
aba_na_iba1 <- sum(is.na(aba$ihc_iba1_ffpe))
aba_complete <- sum(complete.cases(aba))
aba_r_pooled <- cor(aba$ihc_gfap_ffpe, aba$ihc_iba1_ffpe, use = "complete.obs")
aba_r_region <- sapply(split(aba, aba$region), function(s)
  cor(s$ihc_gfap_ffpe, s$ihc_iba1_ffpe, use = "complete.obs"))
```

### Peaks that depend on the settings: spontaneous synaptic currents

Imagine you record from a neuron in a brain slice and, with no stimulation at all, collect the small currents that appear on their own. Each one is the response to neurotransmitter released from a presynaptic terminal. The old question behind this dataset [@paulsen1994] is whether release comes in units. If a synapse releases whole vesicles, amplitudes should come in multiples of one unit: many events of size *q*, fewer of size 2*q*, fewer of 3*q*. Think of buying eggs, which come by the half dozen and the dozen, never by the single yolk. A histogram of amplitudes should then show humps at regular spacing. `guineapig_neuro_df` holds the amplitudes of `r gp_n` spontaneous currents recorded in guinea-pig thalamic slices (the package labels the unit "pA or similar", and I leave the axes in the same words).

This is a dataset where a plain histogram can mislead in both directions, and I want you to see why. A histogram counts events in bins, so you choose the bin width; a density smooths the counts, so you choose the bandwidth. Too wide and a real hump vanishes; too narrow and noise looks like a hump. @fig-eda-ggplot-guineapig draws the same `r gp_n` numbers four ways with `geom_histogram()` and `geom_density()`, changing only that choice.

```{r}
#| label: fig-eda-ggplot-guineapig
#| fig-cap: "Amplitude of spontaneous synaptic currents, drawn four ways. A to C: histograms with bins of 4, 1.5 and 0.3. D: densities with the default smoothing (solid) and with less smoothing (dashed)."
#| fig-alt: "Four panels. A: a coarse histogram with a single hill and a long right tail. B: a medium histogram with a main peak near 7 to 8 and a smaller hump near 15. C: a very fine histogram that looks jagged, with many small spikes. D: two density curves, a smooth one with peaks near 7.5 and 15 and a wavier dashed one with extra small bumps."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# One neutral color for this dataset (not a marker color of this chapter)
gp_color <- "#E69F00"

# A function that draws a histogram of the amplitudes for a chosen bin width
gp_hist <- function(bw, title) {
  ggplot(gp, aes(x = y)) +
    geom_histogram(binwidth = bw, boundary = 0, fill = gp_color,
                   color = "white", alpha = 0.8) +
    labs(title = title, x = "Amplitude", y = "Count") +
    Plot_theme
}

# Three bin widths: too wide, a reasonable middle, too narrow
p_h1 <- gp_hist(4, "Bins of 4")
p_h2 <- gp_hist(1.5, "Bins of 1.5")
p_h3 <- gp_hist(0.3, "Bins of 0.3")

# Two smoothing levels of the density, drawn with different line types
p_d <- ggplot(gp, aes(x = y)) +
  geom_density(aes(linetype = "default smoothing"), fill = gp_color, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_density(aes(linetype = "less smoothing"), adjust = 0.4) +
  scale_linetype_manual(name = NULL,
                        values = c("default smoothing" = "solid",
                                   "less smoothing" = "dashed")) +
  labs(title = "Density", x = "Amplitude", y = "Density") +
  Plot_theme + legend_top()

# Four panels, tagged A to D
(p_h1 | p_h2) / (p_h3 | p_d) + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")
```

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read this figure"}
Compare the panels as if they were four photographs of the same animal taken with different lenses. Ask first what stays the same in all four (here, a big pile at low amplitudes and a long right tail). Then ask which features appear with only one setting. A feature that survives a sensible range of bins or bandwidths deserves attention; one that appears only at the narrowest setting is probably noise, and one that disappears only at the widest is probably just blurred. Never report a hump you found with one setting and could not find with a neighboring one.
:::

What does the dataset say? In panel A the data look like one hill with a tail. In panel B a second hump appears near `r round(gp_peaks[2], 1)`, about twice the position of the main peak at `r round(gp_peaks[1], 1)`, which is the spacing a quantal release would predict. Panel C shows what too little smoothing does: a jagged comb of narrow spikes that tempts you to count peaks that are mostly noise. In panel D the default density keeps the first two humps (at `r round(gp_peaks[1], 1)` and `r round(gp_peaks[2], 1)`), and its third little bump at `r round(gp_peaks[3], 1)` stands on a single measurement (the largest, `r gp_max`; only `r gp_n_top` current exceeds 26), so I do not count it. With less smoothing the dashed curve finds `r length(gp_peaks_narrow)` peaks, and I cannot tell from `r gp_n` currents which of the extra ones are real. That is an honest EDA conclusion: the first two humps are supported, the rest is not, and a stronger claim needs another tool (a mixture model, for instance) and probably more recordings.

One more point about the summary. The mean is `r round(gp_mean, 1)`, the standard deviation `r round(gp_sd, 1)` and the median `r round(gp_median, 1)`. The mean sits between the first and the second hump, in a valley where few currents live, the same trap we met with GFAP at 30 DPI (@fig-eda-ggplot-raincloud). A mean and a standard deviation would tell a reader that the typical current is about `r round(gp_mean)`, and almost no recorded current is typical in that sense.

### Pooling regions: GFAP and IBA1 in human brain tissue

The second dataset brings back our favorite marker in a different tissue. `aba_phenotype_data_df` comes from the Allen Brain Atlas study of aging, dementia and traumatic brain injury [@miller2017]. It has `r aba_n` brain tissue samples from four regions, each quantified by immunohistochemistry for GFAP (astrocytes, as in our mice) and IBA1 (microglia). The package gives only the acronyms, which I read as hippocampus (`HIP`), parietal and temporal neocortex (`PCx`, `TCx`) and forebrain white matter (`FWM`). The staining values have no documented unit, so I keep the axes named after the columns and compare only *between regions*, never against `cell_data`.

The question is the one we asked of time, now asked of region: does the shape of the distribution change from one region to the next? Think of four neighborhoods and their housing prices. A single histogram of the city hides that one neighborhood is cheap and tight and another expensive and spread out. With `r min(aba_n_region)` to `r max(aba_n_region)` samples per region we are well past the thirty-observation rule I gave for showing every point, but the rain is still useful, since it shows where the samples actually fall, and the half-density next to it keeps the shape visible. We use the same raincloud recipe as before, with the regions ordered by median GFAP, blue for GFAP as in the rest of the chapter and a new green for IBA1.

```{r}
#| label: fig-eda-ggplot-aba
#| fig-cap: GFAP and IBA1 immunohistochemistry by brain region in the Allen aging, dementia and TBI samples (raincloud plots; the diamond is the group mean)
#| fig-alt: Two raincloud plots by region (TCx, PCx, HIP, FWM). A, GFAP, climbs from TCx to FWM, with the white matter highest and widest. B, IBA1, is highest and most spread out in the hippocampus, with the other three regions similar. Individual samples appear as points beside each cloud.
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5
#| warning: false
#| message: false

Iba1_color <- "#009E73"

# GFAP by region: cloud, box, rain and mean
aba_gfap <- ggplot(aba, aes(x = region, y = ihc_gfap_ffpe)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5, width = 0.6, .width = 0,
               justification = -0.3, point_colour = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.2, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_half_point(side = "l", range_scale = 0.4, alpha = 0.4) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 18, size = 4, color = Gfap_color) +
  labs(x = "Brain region", y = "GFAP (ihc_gfap_ffpe)") +
  Plot_theme

# IBA1 by region, same layers
aba_iba1 <- ggplot(aba, aes(x = region, y = ihc_iba1_ffpe)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5, width = 0.6, .width = 0,
               justification = -0.3, point_colour = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.2, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_half_point(side = "l", range_scale = 0.4, alpha = 0.4) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 18, size = 4, color = Iba1_color) +
  labs(x = "Brain region", y = "IBA1 (ihc_iba1_ffpe)") +
  Plot_theme

aba_gfap + aba_iba1 + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")
```

@fig-eda-ggplot-aba says different things for the two markers. GFAP climbs from region to region: the median goes from `r sprintf("%.3f", aba_gfap_med[1])` in `r names(aba_gfap_med)[1]` to `r sprintf("%.3f", aba_gfap_med[4])` in `r names(aba_gfap_med)[4]`, and the white matter is also the widest. IBA1 is organized differently: the hippocampus stands out (median `r sprintf("%.3f", aba_iba1_med["HIP"])`, against `r sprintf("%.3f", min(aba_iba1_med[names(aba_iba1_med) != "HIP"]))` to `r sprintf("%.3f", max(aba_iba1_med[names(aba_iba1_med) != "HIP"]))` in the other three regions). A single ranking of "regions by marker" would have been wrong for one of the two. This is the same lesson as the days of `cell_data`: the group is part of the answer, and a pooled figure answers a question nobody asked.

Two checks deserve a place in every EDA of this kind, because the figure alone would not tell you. First, ggplot2 drops missing values silently (we suppressed the warning above): `r aba_na_gfap` samples have no GFAP and `r aba_na_iba1` no IBA1, which leaves `r aba_complete` complete rows out of `r aba_n`, and whether those gaps are harmless is the question of @sec-eda-missing-data. Second, the table has one row per sample and no donor identifier, so I cannot tell which samples came from the same person. If several regions come from one brain, the rows are not independent, and a model that treats them as if they were commits the pseudoreplication that @sec-multilevel-varying-intercepts is about. A figure cannot warn you of that; you have to ask how the data were collected.

For one last look, the scatter of the two markers, split by region (@fig-eda-ggplot-aba-scatter). `facet_wrap()` gives each region its own panel on shared scales, the grown-up version of coloring by day in @fig-cell_data_scatter_covariance_EDA, and it needs no legend because the panel titles already say which region is which.

```{r}
#| label: fig-eda-ggplot-aba-scatter
#| fig-cap: GFAP against IBA1 in each brain region (one point per sample; the line is a straight-line fit)
#| fig-alt: Four scatter plots, one per region (TCx, PCx, HIP, FWM), of GFAP against IBA1. The clouds are broad and sit at different heights in different regions. The straight lines are nearly flat in three regions and slope downward in FWM.
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# One panel per region, same axes, so the clouds can be compared
ggplot(aba, aes(x = ihc_iba1_ffpe, y = ihc_gfap_ffpe)) +
  geom_point(color = Gfap_color, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "black", se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ region) +
  labs(x = "IBA1 (ihc_iba1_ffpe)", y = "GFAP (ihc_gfap_ffpe)") +
  Plot_theme
```

In @fig-eda-ggplot-aba-scatter each region's cloud sits at its own height, and the lines are nearly flat except in `FWM`, where GFAP drifts down as IBA1 rises. Across all samples the correlation between the markers is `r sprintf("%.2f", aba_r_pooled)`; within the regions it is `r paste(sprintf("%.2f", aba_r_region), collapse = ", ")` (in the order `r paste(names(aba_r_region), collapse = ", ")`). None of these is large (the strongest, in `FWM`, is `r sprintf("%.2f", aba_r_region["FWM"])`), and with about 85 samples per region I would not lean on any single one. The lesson is the quieter one: a correlation computed on pooled groups mixes differences *between* groups with association *within* them. We saw the same in `cell_data`, where the days made the two markers move together, and it is why a coefficient on pooled data should be read only after looking at the groups.

## What we have learned about our data

Three questions, three kinds of figure, and one list of findings that will guide every model that follows. These are leads from looking, not results, and they are collected with the rest of the part's findings in @sec-eda-summary.

-   **Scale and shape.** PDGFR-β ranges from `r round(pdgfrb_range[1])` to `r round(pdgfrb_range[2])` and GFAP from `r round(gfap_range[1])` to `r round(gfap_range[2])`, both right-skewed when pooled across days (@fig-cell_data_dens_EDA).
-   **Time trend.** Both markers rise with days post-ischemia, but not along a straight line: PDGFR-β keeps climbing, GFAP plateaus and dips at 30 DPI (@fig-cell_data_scatter_EDA, @fig-cell_data_rain_EDA).
-   **Unequal spread.** Early days (0 and 3 DPI) are tight, later days are widely scattered, which anticipates heteroskedasticity and means one common variance is a poor description.
-   **A summary that misleads.** At 30 DPI, GFAP has two groups of animals and a mean that falls in the gap between them (@fig-cell_data_rain_EDA).
-   **Covariation depends on the day.** The association between the two markers is moderate overall but varies by day, mostly because both markers share the effect of time (@fig-cell_data_scatter_covariance_EDA).

::: {.callout-note title="How to report it"}
**Methods.** Before modeling, we explored the raw data graphically (density plots, scatter plots against days post-ischemia, and raincloud plots showing every animal; n = `r n_obs`, `r min(n_day)` to `r max(n_day)` per day). The standard deviation of GFAP integrated density rose from `r round(gfap_sd_day["0"])` at day 0 to `r round(gfap_sd_day["7"])` at day 7, and that of PDGFR-β integrated density from `r round(pdgfrb_sd_day["0"])` at day 0 to `r round(pdgfrb_sd_day["30"])` at day 30. Because the spread was not constant across days and the trend was not a straight line, we did not rely on a model with one common variance and a linear time trend without checking those assumptions explicitly.
:::

These findings fix the plan. We know that the modeling strategy must allow a trend that is not straight, a variance that changes with time, and a relationship between the markers that depends on the day. Two more tools complete the exploration before we start fitting: @sec-eda-gwalkr lets you explore the same data by dragging variables around, and @sec-eda-ggpairs screens all the pairs of variables at once.
